props.title: Masculin Féminin
props.initialSlug: Youth, sex & politics collide in 1960s Paris

sections.content: Jean-Luc Godard's Masculin Féminin perfectly captures the restless youth culture of 1960s Paris through its provocative blend of documentary-style interviews and fictional narrative. The film follows Paul (Jean-Pierre Léaud), a young intellectual conducting surveys about sex, politics and pop culture with his peers. Godard's approach here influenced later mockumentaries like This Is Spinal Tap (1984) and pseudo-documentary storytelling in films like Medium Cool (1969). The film's famous subtitle "The Children of Marx and Coca-Cola" encapsulates the tension between leftist politics and consumer culture that defined that generation.

sections.content: The film's innovative interview sequences laid groundwork for how cinema could blend fiction and documentary approaches. Later films like No Lies (1973) and Sherman's March (1986) would build on this hybrid format. Godard's rapid-fire editing and jump cuts create a nervous energy that mirrors the cultural upheaval of the period. His influence can be seen in works like Medium Cool (1969), where Haskell Wexler merged scripted drama with actual footage of the 1968 Democratic Convention riots.

The performances, particularly Jean-Pierre Léaud as Paul, showcase the naturalistic acting style that defined French New Wave cinema. Léaud, who began as a child actor in François Truffaut's The 400 Blows (1959), embodies the intellectual yet uncertain youth of the era. His documentary-style interactions with real Parisians blur the line between performance and reality, a technique later directors like Abbas Kiarostami would perfect in films like Close-Up (1990). sections.content: The film's examination of youth culture and political awakening resonated deeply with audiences and influenced later works about generational divide. Films like If.... (1968) and Zabriskie Point (1970) followed similar themes of youth rebellion and political consciousness. Godard's technique of interrupting narrative with documentary elements and political statements influenced countless political filmmakers, from Costa-Gavras to Ken Loach.
